summary:
Orbita is an offline-capable health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts understand their measurements, recognize changes, and find practical guidance during space missions. It combines a personal health assistant with REPER, an English-language crew monitoring dashboard.

Astronauts can record pulse, blood pressure, sleep, mood, and symptoms, while a device API accepts measurements from connected equipment through adapters. The interface explains how to take measurements, highlights results requiring attention, and provides first-aid reference material. A local retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system searches medical instructions and returns source-linked steps.

The project addresses the challenge of crew autonomy when communication with Earth is limited. By presenting measurements alongside their time, location, quality, and context, Orbita helps crew members make more informed decisions and communicate concerns. Our prototype demonstrates these workflows using simulated mission data.
details:
We developed Orbita to support the astronaut’s everyday health routine and the crew leader’s overview of emerging concerns.

The personal application guides astronauts through recording measurements and symptoms. Instructions explain how to measure pulse or use a blood pressure cuff, including how to interpret instrument labels. Each record includes its time, location, source, and measurement conditions. Rule-based checks highlight values requiring review and suggest actions such as repeating a measurement or contacting a crewmate or onboard medic.

Context is central to the design. Pulse readings taken after exercise are distinguished from resting measurements. In our headache demonstration, the application checks whether a recent CO₂ reading exists at the astronaut’s location. A fresh measurement from the base cannot establish conditions inside the rover. The application preserves previous explanations when new evidence arrives.

A medical library provides seven reference guides adapted from CDC, American Heart Association, American Red Cross, and MedlinePlus materials. Its local RAG pipeline uses Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B to retrieve relevant material from a SQLite vector store. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct then selects an applicable guide. The application displays the stored procedure with a citation for each step and reports insufficient evidence when it cannot support an answer. Both models run locally through llama.cpp after installation.

REPER provides a separate English-language monitoring interface with crew summaries, measurement histories, environmental information, and simulated emergency scenarios. The application’s device gateway also supports sharing incoming measurements and urgent requests with the crew leader.

We built the project using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js, Vite, and progressive web application technology. Local storage and caching support continued access to records and reference guides during connectivity loss. The device API includes authentication keys, measurement validation, and duplicate handling.

Our team considered limited communication, non-specialist users, measurement errors, missing or stale data, privacy, and modest onboard computing resources. Personal mood notes require explicit inclusion in exported reports. Clear labels, visible next steps, and source-linked guidance help users understand the basis of a recommendation.

The current prototype uses synthetic mission data and general educational references. Physical devices require model-specific adapters. Photo analysis is planned through a small visual model that will propose an editable description before retrieval; the current RAG interface already accepts a user-confirmed description.

Our intended impact is to help crews notice changes earlier, perform measurements more consistently, and prepare clearer information for medical support during long-duration missions.
